new_data <- polls_us_election_2016

num_cols <- sapply(new_data, is.numeric)
new_data[num_cols] <- lapply(new_data[num_cols], function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- my_birth_year + k
  return(x)
})

char_cols <- sapply(new_data, function(x) is.character(x) | is.factor(x))
new_data[char_cols] <- lapply(new_data[char_cols], function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x) 
  x[is.na(x)] <- paste0(my_first, "_", k)
  return(x)
})

My first assignment has two parts.


Baykal Hafizoglu talks about how he went from working in Industrial Engineering to Optimization Science, specifically at Lamasoft and FICO. He talks about a big project he did for P&G where he turned a 100-line optimization code into software that 200 people use and that is 50,000 lines long. He divides analytics into four types: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive. He stresses that the usefulness of any model depends on how it is used and how it looks.




In the video, Baykal Hafızoğlu emphasizes the relationship between different types of analytics. How does a “Predictive” model’s quality directly affect a “Prescriptive” model, and what example does he give regarding supply chain?

Answer:

According to Hafızoğlu, prescriptive analytics (like optimization) depends on the inputs from predictive analytics (like forecasting). He gives the example of “demand forecasting”; if your demand forecast is poor, the inventory optimization model you build on top of it will produce useless results.

Which type of analytics is focused on providing a “prescription” for a business problem?
a) Descriptive
b) Diagnostic
c) Predictive
d) Prescriptive
Answer: d) Prescriptive
